title: Barclays to cut 5k jobs as bank's bosses hail AI productivity advances
content:
Barclays is cutting 5,000 jobs as part of wider cost-saving plans that its bosses say are being driven by advances in AI.
The job cuts will mean losing about 5% of the bank’s 93,000 global staff, with executives confirming they had already cut 1,000 workers since the start of the year.
The bank’s chief financial officer, Anna Cross, told reporters on Thursday that the job cuts were part of plans to save more than £1.1bn in 2027. “These actions involve an expected reduction of circa 5,000 full-time employees. Around 60% of the group actions relate to support functions, including fewer developers, as AI makes our people more productive.”
When asked how many of the total job cuts would be directly linked to advances in AI, the chief executive, CS Venkatakrishnan, said the bank had been making “deep investments” in technology and simplifying its processes.
“That is driving the bulk of the efficiency gains that you’ve seen so far. AI has an important role to play and may have a more important role to play in the future,” Venkatakrishnan said, calling AI the “icing on the cake” to modernising the bank’s technology.
“We have been focusing on the infrastructure build, and where the infrastructure is modern, we’ve been applying AI.”
The news comes months after another UK-headquartered bank, Standard Chartered, announced plans to cut more than 7,000 jobs over the next four years as it ramps up the use of AI. It will mean slashing about 15% of its back-office roles by 2030.
Barclays also announced plans to hand a further £500m to investors, taking the total amount given to shareholders since January – through buybacks and dividends – to £2.8bn.
It came as the lender reported £2.3bn in pre-tax profits over the July to September quarter, up 12% from £2.1bn during the same period last year.
The strong financial performance will probably to be used to justify the expected increase in bank taxes in the 28 October budget, as Andy Burnham’s government looks for ways to raise revenue to help fund cost of living support programmes.
When asked whether the bank might consider tilting assets or investment out of the UK and to the US – where it also has operations – as a result of higher levies, Venkatakrishnan said the bank would be able to absorb them.
“I recognise that the chancellor and the government … have to balance a host of considerations,” he said, adding that Barclays shared their goal to get growth.
“This is not a question of a financial hit to us. It’s bearable. It is a question of proportion and it’s a question of market signaling. But … I deeply respect the responsibility that the chancellor has and he has our full support and backing.”
Barclays’ strong performance included a 6% rise in net interest income at its UK retail banking operations, to £2bn. The figure has become a flashpoint for campaigners pushing for a bank tax.
It accounts for how much money banks make from loan charges, minus what they pay on deposits, and is linked to interest rates, which have been rising as the Iran war has driven up inflation expectations.
The Trades Union Congress, which has been campaigning for a bank tax increase, said lenders needed to contribute more at a time when people were struggling with household bills.
The TUC general secretary, Paul Nowak, said: “Barclays’ bumper profits aren’t an anomaly. All the big banks are doing exceptionally well … Britain’s big four banks have made £200bn in profit since 2021. They can – and should – pay more tax.”
Healey has promised that next week’s budget will support Britain’s entrepreneurs, and focus on cutting the “cost of business”.
He told the Times: “I want to be a chancellor who backs business in Britain making a profit, those entrepreneurs who in the end are the ones who challenge the status quo, come up with innovative ideas and are trying, some of them through sheer bloody-mindedness, to keep going through these sorts of pressures, which is what they’ve done.”

report.summary: Barclays will cut 5,000 jobs, about 5% of staff, citing cost savings and AI-driven productivity, while reporting higher profits and shareholder returns.
report.background: Barclays’ move reflects a broader cost-cutting wave in banking as lenders invest in cloud, data infrastructure and AI while facing pressure to keep expenses down. Banks have spent years modernising legacy systems; once infrastructure is modern, they can apply AI to support functions, software development and operations. The article frames AI as an accelerant rather than the sole cause: Barclays says simplification and technology investment drive most efficiency gains, with AI playing an important future role. Standard Chartered’s planned 7,000 cuts show similar logic. At the same time, UK banks are reporting strong profits—Barclays’ third-quarter pre-tax profit rose 12% to £2.3bn—and face expected tax increases in the budget, intensifying political scrutiny over whether they should contribute more.
key_points: Barclays plans to cut about 5,000 full-time roles, roughly 5% of its 93,000 global staff, after already reducing 1,000 positions since the start of the year. The cuts are part of a programme to save more than £1.1bn in 2027, with about 60% falling in support functions, including fewer developer roles.

Chief executive CS Venkatakrishnan described AI as the 'icing on the cake' rather than the main driver. He said deep technology investment, infrastructure modernisation and process simplification are delivering most efficiency gains, while AI is already applied where systems are modern and may become more important.

The announcement follows Standard Chartered’s plan to cut more than 7,000 jobs over four years, including about 15% of back-office roles by 2030, as banks increasingly automate support and operations work. The pattern suggests AI adoption is becoming a board-level cost strategy across UK banking.

Barclays reported £2.3bn in pre-tax profit for the July-to-September quarter, up 12% year on year, and said it would return a further £500m to investors. That takes total shareholder returns since January to £2.8bn, a result likely to fuel debate over expected increases in bank taxes.
report.impact: For the AI industry, Barclays is a high-profile proof point that enterprise AI is moving from pilots into workforce and cost planning—though the bank itself says modern infrastructure and simplification do more work than AI alone. For developers, the explicit mention of fewer developer roles signals that support, operations and routine engineering tasks face automation pressure, while AI-augmented engineering and governance skills become more valuable. For regular users, banks may deliver faster, cheaper digital services, but fewer human support staff can mean harder-to-reach help and more automated decision-making. The bigger risk is that productivity gains are used mainly to cut costs and reward shareholders rather than improve services or reskill staff.
report.tools: To follow this trend, watch AI coding assistants such as GitHub Copilot and Cursor, enterprise copilots like Microsoft 365 Copilot, and workflow automation from ServiceNow and UiPath. Open-source options include Continue.dev, OpenHands, LangGraph and n8n for building agents and automations. For enterprise adoption, focus on governance, data security, measurable ROI and human-in-the-loop controls rather than raw seat counts.
